Was Red Bull’s strategy a mistake?
 Isack Hadjar reacts in parc ferme during the São Paulo Grand Prix. Alex Bierens de Haan / Getty Images 
 By Patrick Iversen Nov. 12, 2026 Updated Share article 11 Mercedes sealed the constructors’ championship in Interlagos on Sunday, officially locking down a title double after Kimi Antonelli secured his drivers’ crown in Mexico City.
 Lando Norris captured victory in a wild, wet-dry-wet thriller in São Paulo and Max Verstappen mounted an impressive charge from 21st to second place.
 Advertisement
 We next head to Las Vegas on Nov. 22, where cold weather threatens to turn 2026 tire management into absolute chaos, according to Norris.
 Even with the championships wrapped up, Brazil offered plenty of drama to dissect. Red Bull issued team orders asking Isack Hadjar to yield to Verstappen — a call the pit wall claims they intended to undo had the cars stayed close. Both Antonelli and George Russell fought perplexing handling balance issues that Mercedes engineers are currently analyzing.
 Meanwhile, Liam Lawson’s prospective 2027 Racing Bulls seat stays officially unconfirmed, and Cadillac’s ownership future is firmly in question.
 Let’s jump into your questions about all of that in this week’s mailbag.
 Editor’s note: Questions have been lightly edited for clarity and brevity. 
 Did Red Bull purposely choose the strategy that kept Hadjar behind Verstappen? — Murray C. 
 In a way, yes, but it was not deliberate sabotage. More like … decisions.
 Let’s recap on the key events: On Lap 38, Red Bull told Hadjar to yield position to his teammate so Verstappen could pursue Norris. That backfired – Verstappen didn’t have the pace, leaving Hadjar on his tail, wondering on the radio if he’d get his position back. Team principal Laurent Mekies has since said Red Bull would have swapped them back if the cars had stayed close.
 What You Should Read Next 
 Why Lando Norris and Max Verstappen gave Mercedes a 2027 warning in Brazil
 McLaren and Red Bull are ending 2026 on the up. Just as Mercedes wraps up the F1 teams' title in 2026, it looks vulnerable for 2027.
 But the gap widened when Red Bull pitted Verstappen first on Lap 45, granting him the undercut. Hadjar wanted to stay out to the end of the race, but the team brought him in on Lap 50. Hadjar was again faster than Verstappen, but the five-lap pit delay left him nine seconds adrift. Incoming rain subsequently sealed the running order. 
 Red Bull bet that Verstappen, who had been quick all weekend, would do Max Verstappen things and have the best shot at chasing Norris for the win. It didn’t work and, to be fair, Norris was having a heck of a race out front. I’m not sure either Red Bull would have caught him and Hadjar rightfully earned his podium finish regardless.
 Following another solid performance from Lawson, I suspect the delay in confirming his seat at RB stems from Red Bull waiting to see if he might be placed alongside Verstappen instead of Hadjar. But given that he finished seventh in Brazil, what happens now? Will the current setup across the two teams remain in place? — Andrea D. 
 Well, the Red Bull seat doesn’t explain the wait. Hadjar is already signed alongside Verstappen for 2027, so whatever is holding up Lawson’s confirmation, it isn’t a contest for the senior team. You would think recent race form would have put Lawson in the driver’s seat (pun intended) for the final Racing Bulls seat next year, and rumours suggest that’s the case.
 Advertisement
 As for Lawson’s role at Red Bull, the answer is insurance. When Hadjar was injured, Lawson stepped into the Red Bull for three races. When the junior team needed points, he scored 75, a big reason Racing Bulls sits fifth in the constructors’ championship. He’s earning the company prize money, is a good benchmark for Lindblad and a proven stand-in for the senior team.
 Lawson has more than double the points (89) of rookie teammate Arvid Lindblad (38). (Rudy Carezzevoli / Getty Images) The argument against keeping him is that Racing Bulls exists to develop the next junior, and Nikola Tsolov is next in line. But dropping your best points-scorer for a rookie just as the team has become competitive would be an odd way to run it, in my opinion. But Red Bull has never been less than ruthless about such things.
 For Lawson, devoid of better open seats on the market, Racing Bulls is still the right place, even without a clear path yet. Pierre Gasly’s career should be his model — demoted by Red Bull, rebuilt his reputation enough to sign elsewhere and thrive. Lawson, after all, is only 24.
 So no, he isn’t being held for Red Bull. But he’s most useful to Red Bull, and to himself, where he is. For now.
 Several mistakes from Antonelli in wet conditions (though he blamed a potential suspension issue for some of them). Have we finally found Antonelli’s weakness? — Joydeep B. 
 Was it the wet conditions or tire temperature? Russell was also complaining about similar issues. Some of the drivers seemed able to get the tires to the right temp quickly and evenly across all four tires. It seemed to me (based on Sky Sports commentary as my only basis) that they were both struggling with tire temp. That said, given the lack of wet races this year, he certainly has a lot less experience in those conditions in an F1 car. Hopefully Las Vegas will be cool and deliver some rain, as that would be telling. Maybe it’s track limits and wet/cool conditions for Kimi? — Momy B. 
 The wet part of the afternoon was actually Antonelli’s best! On intermediates, he passed Norris at the start and built a lead of around eight seconds. The trouble began when the track dried and Mercedes put him on slicks. He told his engineer right away that the rear felt wrong, then spun at Turn 1 and handed Norris the lead. With all four tires flat-spotted, his pace didn’t come back until his next set of softs.
 Advertisement
 Momy is onto something, too. Russell spun in the pit lane moments after his own switch to slicks, and both drivers reported the same strange behavior.
 Mercedes’ Italian driver Kimi Antonelli leads the pack at the start of Sunday’s race in Brazil. (Maruo Pimentel / AFP via Getty Images) But yes, usually, when two drivers on the same team report similar issues, it’s the machines under them rather than their skill set. So the evidence points at the car and tires on a drying track, not at Antonelli in the rain.
 That doesn’t make him flawless, though. He’s young, and 2026 hasn’t offered many wet races to learn from. It very well could be a weakness! We just haven’t seen him battle in the wet enough to make a call.
 Is it time to revisit the ‘random sprinkler’ idea? I joke, but it’s wild how much better the racing is when the conditions change throughout the race. The closest thing we have to a random, race-changing event right now is Stroll retiring at varying times every race. — Luco O. 
 I’m so glad you brought this up because it’s one of my favorite “F1 is a silly-sport, actually” moments.
 For those who don’t know, in 2011 Bernie Ecclestone proposed sprinklers that would come on at unannounced times during a race. Let’s sit with that a moment.
 OK, now let’s unpack. Rather obvious why it never actually happened: If drivers think the battery-led engines of 2026 make racing artificial, imagine the uproar if artificial rain was introduced at random times. And the first person who gets injured because of it.
 It also wouldn’t work as well as you’d hope. You see, the sun is very powerful. How many sprinklers are we talking about? Because the sun, firing off one hundred octillion microscopic fusion reactions per nanosecond, will dry the surface pretty quickly.
 Rafael Camara of Brazil driving in the rain during qualifying for the grand prix. (Alex Pantling / Getty Images) So now we’re in a When-You-Give-A-Mouse-A-Cookie situation: If you want artificial wet surfaces, you’re going to need some artificial clouds. And if you have artificial clouds, the FIA now has a Weather Director, and Toto Wolff is on the phone mid-race asking why the cumulonimbus over Turn 4 started pouring the exact lap both Mercedes pitted for slicks. Just a mess.
 Advertisement
 Or, as Josh M. suggested elsewhere in the mailbag, we could skip all that and just race at Interlagos, where the sky does this for free.
 And Luco, you’ve identified what makes these races great: uncertainty. An F1 strategy is a finely made clock, plans built on plans built on plans. Rain throws a wrench into the gears. At Interlagos, every team had to start guessing and committing to calls on the fly. It was fun. Sometimes the best thing for this perfectly engineered sport is a little mess.
